questions.q: What is the main idea of @zudojs/storage?
questions.explain: Your app depends on what storage does (Database, ObjectStorage, LockManager…), not on what it is. To move files from disk to a cloud bucket, you write a new ObjectStorage, and nothing else changes.
options: It is a faster PostgreSQL driver
It defines small contracts (interfaces) for storage, and your code depends only on those, not on one driver
It replaces your database with files on disk
It generates SQL tables from TypeScript types

questions.q: Which contract comes without a ready-made implementation, so you write a small adapter for your driver?
questions.explain: ObjectStorage has LocalObjectStorage, Serializer has JsonSerializer and LockManager has InMemoryLockManager. For Database you write an adapter, like the lesson's PgliteDatabase.
options: Database
ObjectStorage
Serializer
LockManager

questions.q: In the Database contract, a query is an object: { text, parameters }. Why does that help security?
questions.explain: The contract has no method that takes one SQL string with values inside. Values always go in parameters as $1, $2…, so user input cannot become SQL.
options: It encrypts the SQL before it is sent
SQL text and values travel apart, so there is no way to call it with values glued into the SQL
It makes every query read-only
It checks that the table exists before running

questions.q: The PgliteDatabase adapter writes savepoint names straight into SQL: SAVEPOINT "${name}". What is the rule for those names?
questions.explain: A name is part of the SQL text, not a parameter. A name made by an attacker could close the quote and add their own SQL. Use fixed names written in your code.
options: Any name is fine, because it is inside double quotes
Only pass names from your own code, never from a request
Names must come from the request, so each user has their own savepoint
Always use the user's id as the name

questions.q: What should rowCount report for an UPDATE in the lesson's adapter?
questions.explain: A SELECT reports the rows it returned; INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE report the rows they changed. That is why the adapter uses affectedRows when there are no result fields.
options: The number of rows in the whole table
The number of rows it changed
Always 1
The number of columns it changed

questions.q: The fake database below prints the query the repository sends. What does this print?
questions.explain: Values become $1, $2 parameters, in order: first the new value, then the id. The column name done is written into the SQL, which is why it must be on the allow-list.
options: UPDATE tasks SET done = $1 WHERE id = $2 RETURNING * [ true, 1 ]
UPDATE tasks SET done = true WHERE id = 1 RETURNING * []
UPDATE tasks SET done = $1 WHERE id = $2 RETURNING * [ 1, true ]
UPDATE tasks SET $1 = $2 WHERE id = $3 RETURNING * [ 'done', true, 1 ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Limit and offset are values, so they are parameters. The sort column is a name, not a value, so it goes into the SQL text, after the allow-list check.
options: SELECT * FROM tasks ORDER BY title DESC LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2 [ 5, 10 ]
SELECT * FROM tasks ORDER BY $1 DESC LIMIT $2 OFFSET $3 [ 'title', 5, 10 ]
SELECT * FROM tasks ORDER BY title DESC LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10 []
SELECT * FROM tasks ORDER BY title DESC LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2 [ 10, 5 ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The filter value 'ada' is a parameter. The repository returns the count from the row, which is 2 here.
options:
SELECT COUNT(*) as count FROM tasks WHERE owner_id = $1 [ 'ada' ]
2

SELECT COUNT(*) as count FROM tasks WHERE owner_id = 'ada' []
2

SELECT COUNT(*) as count FROM tasks WHERE owner_id = $1 [ 'ada' ]
1

SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE owner_id = $1 [ 'ada' ]
2

questions.q: A client sends { "is_admin": true } and a careless route passes it to update. What does this print?
questions.explain: is_admin is not in columns, so the repository refuses it with a 400 before any SQL is sent.
options: 400 STORAGE_IDENTIFIER_NOT_ALLOWED
query sent
500 STORAGE_QUERY_FAILED
403 STORAGE_FORBIDDEN

questions.q: A client puts SQL into the title. What does this print?
questions.explain: The value is a parameter, so PostgreSQL stores it as an odd title and nothing else changes. That is exactly right: values never need escaping by hand when they are parameters.
options: UPDATE tasks SET title = $1 WHERE id = $2 RETURNING * [ "x', owner_id = 'mallory", 1 ]
UPDATE tasks SET title = 'x', owner_id = 'mallory' WHERE id = 1 RETURNING * []
UPDATE tasks SET title = $1, owner_id = $2 WHERE id = $3 RETURNING * [ 'x', 'mallory', 1 ]
STORAGE_SQL_INJECTION

questions.q: A route passes the request body to tasks.update(id, body). The body is { "done": true, "owner_id": "mallory" }, and owner_id is on the repository's columns list. What happens?
questions.explain: This is mass assignment. owner_id must be on the list so your own code can set it. The allow-list is a safety net for SQL, not a permission system.
options: The repository refuses it, because clients may not change owners
The update succeeds and Mallory now owns the task: the allow-list cannot know who the caller is
PostgreSQL refuses it with a permission error
Only done is saved; owner_id is ignored

questions.q: What is the right fix for the mass-assignment bug?
questions.explain: The fix belongs at the edge of your app. A .strict() schema answers 400 for any unknown key such as owner_id, and the owner always comes from the session, never from the body.
options: Remove owner_id from columns
Escape the body with JSON.stringify first
Validate the body with a strict schema that accepts only fields a client may change, and set the owner on the server from the logged-in user
Check that owner_id is a valid user id

questions.q: Finish taskChanges(body), a plain-JavaScript version of a strict schema. A client may change only title and done. If the body has any other key, return { status: 400, unknown: [...] } listing those keys. Otherwise return { status: 200, changes } with only the allowed keys that are present.
questions.explain: Refuse unknown keys instead of silently dropping them: the client learns its request was wrong, and owner_id never gets near the database.

questions.q: Finish newTaskRow(body, user). It builds the row to insert: title (trimmed) and done (default false) come from the body, but owner_id always comes from the logged-in user.id, whatever the body says.
questions.explain: Pick each field on purpose instead of spreading the body ({ ...body }), which would copy owner_id from the client. The owner is the server's decision.
questions.expected:
{ title: 'Buy milk', done: false, owner_id: 'ada' }
{ title: 'Steal', done: true, owner_id: 'ada' }

questions.q: Parsed data can hold keys whose value is undefined, like { title: undefined, done: true }. Passed to an update, such a key could set the column to NULL. Finish definedOnly(data) so it returns a copy without those keys. Keep null and false: they are real values.
questions.explain: Object.entries, a filter on value !== undefined, then Object.fromEntries. A check like if (value) would wrongly drop false and null.
questions.expected:
{ done: true }
{ title: 'Buy milk', done: false, note: null }

questions.q: A client asks to sort by id. What does this print?
questions.explain: A name with ; and spaces is not even a valid identifier. id is valid, but not on the columns list, so it is refused too. The allow-list is used for writes, filters and sorting alike.
options:
title; DROP TABLE tasks STORAGE_INVALID_IDENTIFIER
id STORAGE_IDENTIFIER_NOT_ALLOWED
title ok

title; DROP TABLE tasks STORAGE_INVALID_IDENTIFIER
id ok
title ok

title; DROP TABLE tasks ok
id STORAGE_IDENTIFIER_NOT_ALLOWED
title ok

title; DROP TABLE tasks STORAGE_IDENTIFIER_NOT_ALLOWED
id STORAGE_IDENTIFIER_NOT_ALLOWED
title STORAGE_IDENTIFIER_NOT_ALLOWED

questions.q: You want clients to sort by id, so you add id to columns. What else changes?
questions.explain: The same list controls writes, filters and sorting. With a strict schema at the edge that is harmless; without one, id is one more field a client could change.
options: Nothing else changes
update would now accept a new id too, so a strict schema at the edge becomes even more important
The repository stops using parameters for id
findById stops working

questions.q: Where should a task's PDF attachment go?
questions.explain: Databases are for rows; files go into object storage. An object is the file plus a little metadata, stored under a key. Cloud services such as Amazon S3 work the same way.
options: In a text column of the tasks table
In object storage, under a key like tasks/1/<id>, with its content type and size as metadata
In an environment variable
In the lock manager

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: put returns the object's metadata: key, size in bytes (8 for "Oat milk") and content type. get returns null for a missing key, so your route can answer 404.
options:
tasks/1/notes.txt 8 text/plain
missing: null

tasks/1/notes.txt 8 text/plain
missing: undefined

notes.txt 8 text/plain
missing: null

tasks/1/notes.txt 8 text/plain
NotFoundError: tasks/9/nothing.txt

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: list(prefix) finds every key that starts with the text. "tasks/10/c.txt" starts with "tasks/1", so end your prefix with / to list one task only.
options:
[ 'tasks/1/a.txt' ]
[ 'tasks/1/a.txt', 'tasks/10/c.txt' ]

[ 'tasks/1/a.txt' ]
[ 'tasks/1/a.txt' ]

[ 'tasks/1/a.txt', 'tasks/10/c.txt' ]
[ 'tasks/1/a.txt', 'tasks/10/c.txt' ]

[ 'a.txt' ]
[ 'a.txt', 'c.txt' ]

questions.q: A task has 2500 attachments. files.list("tasks/1/") returns 1000 objects and isTruncated: true. What do you do?
questions.explain: list returns at most maxKeys objects (1000 by default). The continuationToken tells the next call where to go on, like a cursor.
options: Nothing: the other 1500 are lost
Call list again with the continuationToken it returned, until isTruncated is false
Delete 1500 objects so the list fits
Call list with a bigger folder name

questions.q: put also computes an etag, a SHA-256 hash of the content. What is it useful for?
questions.explain: A hash is a fingerprint of the bytes. Same content, same etag; change one byte and the etag changes. It is not encryption and says nothing about who uploaded it.
options: Encrypting the file
Telling whether a file changed: different content gives a different etag
Choosing the file's key
Proving who uploaded the file

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A key with .. would climb out of the storage folder (path traversal), so it is refused with 400. A file larger than maxObjectBytes gets 413 Payload Too Large.
options:
400 STORAGE_PATH_TRAVERSAL
413 STORAGE_OBJECT_TOO_LARGE
stored

stored
413 STORAGE_OBJECT_TOO_LARGE
stored

400 STORAGE_PATH_TRAVERSAL
stored
stored

404 STORAGE_NOT_FOUND
413 STORAGE_OBJECT_TOO_LARGE
stored

questions.q: What can a path traversal attack do if keys are not checked?
questions.explain: On disk a key becomes a path, and .. climbs out of the folder. With enough ../, a key reaches anywhere your server process can write or read.
options: Only make the file name longer
Read or overwrite any file the server can reach, such as /etc/passwd or your source code
Slow down the upload
Nothing, because the files are in a temporary folder

questions.q: A user uploads holiday photo.png to task 7. Which key is best?
questions.explain: Don't use a user's file name as the key: make the key yourself, so it is always safe and never collides. Keep the original name in the metadata for display. Also check that the user may touch task 7.
options: holiday photo.png
tasks/7/holiday photo.png
tasks/7/<a random UUID>, with the original name kept in the metadata
<the user's id>/holiday photo.png

questions.q: Finish attachmentKey(taskId, fileName, id). Throw RangeError("taskId must be a positive whole number") unless taskId is a safe integer of at least 1. Return { key, metadata } where key is tasks/<taskId>/<id> and metadata.fileName is the original name cut to 200 characters. (In the app, id comes from randomUUID().)
questions.explain: The dangerous name is kept only as metadata; the key is built from values you control. Number.isSafeInteger refuses 1.5 and the string "1".
questions.expected:
{ key: 'tasks/1/3f1c', metadata: { fileName: '../../secret.txt' } }
RangeError taskId must be a positive whole number
RangeError taskId must be a positive whole number
RangeError taskId must be a positive whole number

questions.q: What does plain JSON do to these values?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify turns a Date into a string and a Set into an empty object. After parsing you get a plain string and {} back, and the tags are gone.
questions.code:
const snapshot = { due: new Date(0), tags: new Set(["home"]), views: 1 };
console.log(JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(snapshot)));
options: { due: {}, tags: {}, views: 1 }

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The result is bytes (Uint8Array), ready for object storage or a cache. Each special value is tagged with $type, so deserialize knows what to rebuild.
options:
Uint8Array
{"due":{"$type":"Date","$value":"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"},"views":{"$type":"BigInt","$value":"12"}}

Buffer
{"due":{"$type":"Date","$value":0},"views":{"$type":"BigInt","$value":12}}

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JsonSerializer keeps Date, Set, Map and BigInt through the round trip to bytes, thanks to the $type tags.
options: true true 1
false false undefined
true false undefined
false true 1

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JsonSerializer only speaks JSON. Asking for another format throws a StorageError that says so, instead of silently writing JSON.
options: StorageError
serialized
TypeError
SyntaxError

questions.q: Two requests edit task 1 at the same moment: both read it, both change it, both save. What goes wrong without a lock?
questions.explain: This is the lost update. A lock lets only one request work on the task at a time, so the second one reads the first one's result before changing it.
options: The database crashes
The first change is lost, because the second save overwrites it
Both changes are merged automatically
The second request gets a 409 by itself

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: tryAcquire gives up at once and returns null while the lock is held. After the release, the next lock gets a bigger fence (2). The old lock no longer holds it.
options:
1 null
2 false true

1 null
1 false true

1 undefined
2 false true

1 null
2 true true

questions.q: The first holder is too slow and its lock's TTL runs out. What does this print?
questions.explain: After 30 ms the slow holder's lock expired, so the fast one got it, with fence 2. The slow worker may not notice; that is why the protected store must refuse writes with an older fence.
options: false 1 2
true 1 2
false 1 1
true 1 1

questions.q: Why does every lock have a ttl (time to live)?
questions.explain: A crashed process never calls release(). The TTL makes sure the lock is freed anyway. The price is that a slow (not crashed) holder can lose its lock, which fencing handles.
options: To make locks faster
If the holder crashes, the lock expires and others can go on, instead of waiting forever
So that the lock can be shared by two holders
To decide the fence number

questions.q: Finish save(title, fence) in TaskStore. If fence is smaller than the highest fence seen so far, throw new Error(`stale fence ${fence}, current is ${this.highestFence}`). Otherwise remember the fence and save the title.
questions.explain: Every new lock gets a bigger fence, so a write with an older fence comes from a holder that lost its lock. Refusing it keeps the newer work safe.
questions.expected:
stale fence 1, current is 2
title: Buy soy milk

questions.q: You run three copies of your server behind a load balancer, each with an InMemoryLockManager. What do the locks protect?
questions.explain: An in-memory lock lives in one process. For several servers, use a lock they share, such as PostgreSQL advisory locks via createLockManager from @zudojs/database, or a LockManager over Redis.
options: Everything: the copies share their memory
Only work inside the same process; two copies can hold "the same" lock at once
Only the first copy that started
Nothing on the first request, then everything

questions.q: Finish withLock(locks, key, work): acquire the lock, run work(lock.fence) and return its result, and always release the lock, even when work throws. The small locks object below prints when it acquires and releases.
questions.explain: try { return await work(…) } finally { release } is the pattern. The await inside try matters: without it, finally would run before the work finishes.
questions.expected:
acquire task:1
release task:1
saved with fence 1
acquire task:2
release task:2
work failed

questions.q: The pool has min: 1, max: 2. What does this print?
questions.explain: min: 1 opens one connection at start. The second is opened when needed, and never more than max: 2. The third acquire waits, and gets conn-1 as soon as it is released.

questions.q: Why should you prefer pool.use(fn) over acquire() and release()?
questions.explain: use acquires, runs your function and releases in a finally. With manual acquire, one missed release on an error path slowly drains the pool.
options: It is the only way to run a query
It always gives the connection back, even when fn throws; a forgotten release loses that connection for good
It opens a new connection for every call
It retries failed queries

questions.q: All connections are busy, and a request has waited longer than acquireTimeout. Why is it good that it fails instead of waiting forever?
questions.explain: A request that waits forever holds memory and a client connection. Failing fast gives a quick error, and the server stays responsive for the rest.
options: It is not good: requests should always wait
Under heavy load, failing fast stops requests from piling up and using memory while they wait
So that the pool can open more than max connections
Because the database closes waiting connections anyway

questions.q: When do you call pool.drain()?
questions.explain: drain() lets running work finish and then closes every connection, which is what a clean shutdown needs.
options: Before every query
On shutdown: it waits for connections in use, then closes them all
When a query fails
Every minute, to free memory

questions.q: What does StorageLifecycleManager do?
questions.explain: Storage has to start before the server takes requests and stop after the last one. The manager runs those steps for every component that implements StorageLifecycle.
options: It backs up the database every night
It runs initialize and start for every registered component before requests, and drain and shutdown when the app stops
It decides which user may use which storage
It picks the fastest storage for each query

questions.q: One component is healthy and one is not. What does this print?
questions.explain: The report is unhealthy as a whole when any component is, and it names which one. Your /health route turns that into a 503, while the details go to your logs.
options: false [ 'files' ]
true [ 'files' ]
false []
true []

questions.q: Finish healthResponse(components). Each item is { name, healthy, status }. Answer { status: 200, body: { healthy: true } } when all are healthy. Otherwise answer 503 with body: { healthy: false, failing: [names] }. Never put the status texts in the body: they can hold internal details.
questions.explain: Healthy only when every component is. The public body names what is failing, while the detailed texts (like a folder path) stay in your logs.
questions.expected:
{ status: 200, body: { healthy: true } }
{ status: 503, body: { healthy: false, failing: [ 'files' ] } }

questions.q: Your app uses LocalObjectStorage. Next month you move files to a cloud bucket. If your code depends only on the ObjectStorage contract, what must change?
questions.explain: That is the point of contracts: code that calls put, get and list does not care where the bytes live. You swap the implementation in one place, as with the dependency container.
options: Every route that reads or writes files
Only the place that creates the storage: you pass a new ObjectStorage implementation there
The database schema
Nothing, LocalObjectStorage uploads to the cloud by itself
